column2: picnics

column1: «Buona Pasqua!» dice Samira. «Ho portato tutto per domani.»
column2: “Happy Easter!” Samira says. “I've brought everything for tomorrow.”
column4: Easter — The most important holiday of the Italian spring; Easter Sunday.

column1: «Lucia,» dice Leo. «Perché si chiama Pasquetta?»
column2: “Lucia,” Leo says. “Why is it called Pasquetta?”
column4: Easter Monday — The Monday after Easter: a national holiday for picnics and day trips.

column1: «Nadia,» dice piano. «Ti ricordi la colomba dell'anno scorso?»
column2: “Nadia,” she says softly. “Do you remember the colomba from last year?”
column4: dove-shaped Easter cake — A cake shaped like a dove, the Easter cousin of panettone.

column1: Leo rientra con un uovo di cioccolato grande in due mani.
column2: Leo comes back in with a big chocolate egg in both hands.
column4: chocolate egg — Italian children get a big chocolate egg with a surprise inside.

column1: «Ah, sì! Il picnic!» dice. «Domani, Pasquetta, tutti al lago.»
column2: “Oh, yes! The picnic!” he says. “Tomorrow, Easter Monday, everybody to the lake.”
column4: picnic — Invariable: il picnic, i picnic.

column1: «Mezz'ora?» chiede Kevin. «Per andare in campagna?»
column2: “Half an hour?” Kevin asks. “To get to the campagna?”
column4: countryside — Don't confuse with la compagna (classmate, female friend).

column1: «Buongiorno,» dice. «La strada per il lago è corta. Mezz'ora.»
column2: “Good morning,” he says. “The road to the lago is short. Half an hour.”
column4: lake — The picnic is by a lake in the countryside.

column1: Leo cerca dentro il cestino di Kevin con due mani.
column2: Leo searches inside Kevin's cestino with both hands.
column4: basket — Il cestino del picnic: the picnic basket.

column1: «Di colombe,» dice Nadia. «E di bibite. E di frittata.»
column2: “About colombe,” Nadia says. “And about bibita. And about frittata.”
column4: omelette — A cold frittata is classic Easter Monday food.

column1: Kevin ha già messo nel bagagliaio il cestino, l'insalata e le bibite.
column2: Kevin has already put the cestino, the insalata and the bibite in the trunk.
column4: salad — Insalata di riso is the classic Italian picnic salad.

column1: Sopra tutto c'è un panorama grande, con le montagne piccole in fondo.
column2: Above everything there's a big panorama, with the mountains small in the distance.
column4: view, scenery — What you look at from the top of a hill.

column1: Ornella intanto piega la tovaglia con molta attenzione, in quattro.
column2: Meanwhile Ornella folds the tovaglia very carefully, in four.
column4: tablecloth — At a picnic it goes on the grass, not on a table.

column1: Emma e Tommaso camminano verso la riva.
column2: Emma and Tommaso walk toward the riva.
column4: shore, bank — La riva del lago: where the water meets the land.

column1: La terza boccia è finita nel bosco, e nessuno l'ha trovata.
column2: The third ball ended up in the bosco, and nobody has found it.
column4: woods — Smaller than a forest, bigger than a garden.

column1: «Di colombe,» dice Nadia. «E di bibite. E di frittata.»
column2: “About colombe,” Nadia says. “And about bibita. And about frittata.”
column4: soft drink, soda — Cold drinks for a picnic, usually in a bottle.

column1: Trova la borraccia di Leo vicino al cartello del sentiero.
column2: He finds Leo's borraccia near the sentiero sign.
column4: water bottle — The reusable bottle everybody carries to school or on a trip.

column1: «Papà! C'è la sorpresa dentro?» chiede Leo.
column2: “Dad! Is the surprise inside?” Leo asks.
column4: surprise — Something you don't expect, good or bad.

column1: «Il vento,» dice Franco. «Il vento ha girato.»
column2: “The vento,” Franco says. “The wind turned.”
column4: wind — On a lake, the wind arrives in the afternoon.

column1: Nel cielo arriva una nuvola bianca, grande e bassa.
column2: A big, low white nuvola arrives in the sky.
column4: cloud — A white nuvola is fine; a grey one is not.

column1: Sulla riva passa piano una barca, con un uomo e un cane.
column2: On the riva a barca passes slowly, with a man and a dog.
column4: boat — Small boats on the lake, for fishing or for a ride.

column1: Trova la borraccia di Leo vicino al cartello del sentiero.
column2: He finds Leo's borraccia near the sentiero sign.
column4: path — A narrow path through the woods or along the water.

column1: «Allora l'ombrellone vola,» dice. «E vola verso il lago.»
column2: “Then the ombrellone flies,” Franco says. “And it flies toward the lake.”
column4: beach umbrella — The big one, not the rain umbrella (ombrello).

column1: Marina nota i due ragazzi sulla riva e sorride.
column2: Marina notices the two kids on the riva and smiles.
column4: to notice — Notare is to see something and think about it.

column1: «Matteo,» dice. «Hai già comprato il pane per domani?»
column2: “Matteo,” she says. “Have you already bought the bread for tomorrow?”
column4: already — Ho già preparato tutto: the adverb goes between avere and the participle.

column1: «Ho appena capito le regole!» dice Kevin. «Credo.»
column2: “I've just understood the rules!” Kevin says. “I think.”
column4: just, just now — Ho appena finito: it happened a minute ago.

column1: «E una barca come quella, cinquant'anni fa?» chiede Chiara.
column2: “And a boat like that one, fifty years ago?” Chiara asks.
column4: ago — Two days fa, a year fa: it goes after the time expression.

column1: «Non ancora, mamma,» dice. «Dopo. Adesso ho lo stomaco chiuso.»
column2: “Not yet, Mom,” she says. “Later. Right now my stomach is closed.”
column4: not yet — Non ho ancora mangiato: ancora goes after non.

column1: «Bella giornata,» dice Matteo. «Meglio dell'anno scorso.»
column2: “Beautiful day,” Matteo says. “Better than last year.”
column4: last — L'anno scorso, la settimana scorsa: it agrees with the noun.
